questions.prompt: The ideal reference has zero specimen compliance. What additive displacement offset in mm follows from the mean ref00 report at zero force? Enter the number only.

questions.prompt: An ideal synthetic rocket starts at 600 kg and ends at 450 kg. Its exhaust speed relative to the rocket is constant at 800 m/s, and external forces are negligible. What is its velocity increment? Enter the number in m/s.

questions.prompt: At one instant, a synthetic rocket has mass 500 kg, exhaust speed relative to it u = 300 m/s, positive mass-loss rate q = 4 kg/s and external force −200 N. What is its acceleration along the positive axis? Enter the signed value in m/s².

feedback.hint: With q positive for outflow, m a = Fext + u q.

questions.prompt: A rocket moves at +50 m/s in an inertial frame. Gas leaves backward at 300 m/s relative to the rocket. What is the gas velocity in the inertial frame?

feedback.hint: Convert relative velocity to the stated inertial frame.
feedback.solution: The backward relative velocity is −300 m/s, so wout = 50−300 = −250 m/s.

questions.prompt: A 20 kg cart moves at 10 m/s on a low-friction track and captures 5 kg of pellets initially at rest, retaining them. If external horizontal impulse is negligible, what is the cart-plus-pellet speed afterward?

feedback.hint: Conserve momentum for the cart and pellets together during the brief capture.

questions.prompt: Which statements about one-dimensional variable-mass momentum are correct? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Keep each stream velocity in the same inertial frame and keep inflow and outflow separate.
feedback.solution: Mass-flow terms carry momentum; a body can change velocity as it captures material; and rocket exhaust velocity must be converted from the rocket frame.

options: The body momentum changes due to external force and the momentum carried across its boundary.
All stream velocities must be expressed in the same inertial frame.
A zero net mass rate guarantees that incoming and outgoing momentum fluxes cancel.
Incoming mass at rest can slow a moving body that captures and retains it.
Rocket exhaust inertial velocity is v−u when u is its backward relative speed.
The fixed-mass expression Fext=m a can always be used without flux terms.

questions.prompt: When is Δv = u ln(m0/mf) the appropriate ideal rocket velocity increment?

feedback.hint: Check the assumptions used when integrating the rocket equation.
feedback.solution: The relation assumes one-dimensional motion, constant relative exhaust speed and negligible external force; it is an ideal velocity increment.

options: One-dimensional motion, constant relative exhaust speed, and negligible external force.
Any exhaust speed and arbitrary external force, because mass ratio determines everything.
A constant propellant rate is required, but no condition on exhaust speed is needed.
The equation predicts thrust power and structural loads without further modeling.

questions.prompt: For a body with streams crossing its boundary, which one-dimensional momentum balance uses positive mass-rate magnitudes and inertial-frame stream velocities?

feedback.hint: Use the body momentum rate, external force and signed incoming/outgoing fluxes.
feedback.solution: d(mv)/dt = Fext + Σin mdot_in win − Σout mdot_out wout.

options: d(mv)/dt = Fext + Σin mdot_in win − Σout mdot_out wout.
d(mv)/dt = Fext + Σin mdot_in win + Σout mdot_out wout.
m dv/dt = Fext for all open bodies.

questions.prompt: An ideal rocket ejects material at the same velocity as the rocket in the inertial frame. With no external force, what acceleration follows from the momentum-flux model?

feedback.hint: The exhaust has no relative velocity to the rocket, so inspect the outflow momentum relative to the body.
feedback.solution: If wout=v, the relative outflow term is zero; absent external force, the rocket has no acceleration in this ideal model.

options: It accelerates because losing mass always increases speed.
It accelerates backward because no gas is expelled relative to it.
It has zero acceleration in this model.
Its acceleration cannot be related to momentum.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Two uniform spheres of 50 kg and 80 kg have centres 0.50 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them, in μN? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use F = Gm₁m₂/r² with r between the centres.
feedback.solution: F = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 50 × 80/0.25 = 1.07 × 10⁻⁶ N = 1.07 μN, far too small to notice in everyday handling.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and a synthetic spherical, non-rotating planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m, with no atmosphere. What is the gravitational field strength 2.0 × 10⁶ m above the surface, in m/s²? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Measure r from the centre: r = R + h.
feedback.solution: g = GM/r² = 4.0 × 10¹⁴/(8.4 × 10⁶)² = 5.67 m/s², about 58% of the surface value.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and a synthetic spherical, non-rotating planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m, with no atmosphere. A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.2 × 10⁷ m measured from the planet's centre. What is its speed, in km/s? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Set GMm/r² = mv²/r; the satellite's mass cancels.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and a synthetic spherical, non-rotating planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m, with no atmosphere. A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.2 × 10⁷ m measured from the planet's centre. What is its period, in minutes? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: T = 2πr/v, or Kepler's third law T² = 4π²r³/GM.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and a synthetic spherical, non-rotating planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m, with no atmosphere. What circular-orbit radius gives a period of exactly 12 h, in units of 10⁶ m? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Rearrange Kepler's third law: r = (GM T²/4π²)^(1/3) with T in seconds.
feedback.solution: T = 43 200 s, so r = (4.0 × 10¹⁴ × 43 200²/4π²)^(1/3) = 2.66 × 10⁷ m, about 4.2 planetary radii.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and a synthetic spherical, non-rotating planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m, with no atmosphere. A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.2 × 10⁷ m measured from the planet's centre. What is the escape speed from that radius, in km/s? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Set ½mv² − GMm/r = 0.
feedback.solution: v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2 × 5.775 = 8.17 km/s; the satellite needs about 2.39 km/s more along its motion.

questions.prompt: Stipulate G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² and a synthetic spherical, non-rotating planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m, with no atmosphere. A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 1.2 × 10⁷ m measured from the planet's centre. The satellite's mass is 200 kg. What is its total mechanical energy, with zero potential energy at infinite separation, in GJ? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: For a circular orbit, E = −GMm/(2r).
feedback.solution: E = −4.0 × 10¹⁴ × 200/(2 × 1.2 × 10⁷) = −3.34 × 10⁹ J. The kinetic energy is +3.34 GJ and the potential energy −6.67 GJ.

questions.prompt: Satellite B orbits the same planet in a circle of four times the radius of satellite A. How many times longer is B's period? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: T is proportional to r^(3/2).
feedback.solution: 4^(3/2) = 8. B is also slower, by a factor √4 = 2, and travels four times as far per revolution.

questions.prompt: Two satellites of 100 kg and 2000 kg share the same circular orbit radius around a planet. How do their speeds compare?
options: They are equal, because the satellite's mass cancels between GMm/r² and mv²/r
The heavier one is faster, because gravity pulls it harder
The lighter one is faster, because it has less inertia
They cannot share an orbit

feedback.hint: Write the inward force equation for each and divide by m.
feedback.solution: Gravity's pull and the required centripetal force both scale with m, so v = √(GM/r) for any satellite mass, as long as the satellite's mass is negligible compared with the planet's.

questions.prompt: Why do astronauts in a low circular orbit feel weightless?
options: They and their spacecraft are in free fall together; gravity is still about 80–90% of its surface value
They are beyond the reach of the planet's gravity
The centrifugal force exactly cancels gravity on them in an inertial frame
There is no air in orbit to press on them

feedback.hint: What force acts on an orbiting astronaut, and what does it do?
feedback.solution: Gravity is the only force and supplies the centripetal acceleration. Because the cabin accelerates identically, the floor exerts no contact force, which is what the sensation of weight comes from.

questions.prompt: A satellite moves from a lower circular orbit to a higher one. What happens to its speed and its total mechanical energy?
options: Its speed decreases, but its total energy increases
Its speed and total energy both decrease
Its speed and total energy both increase
Its speed increases, but its total energy decreases

feedback.hint: Compare v = √(GM/r) and E = −GMm/(2r) as r grows.
feedback.solution: v falls as r grows, but E = −GMm/(2r) becomes less negative, so energy must be added: the potential-energy gain is twice the kinetic-energy loss.

feedback.solution: For P, ω = √(3924/0.090) = 208.81 rad/s, or about 1,994 rpm. Since ω²r is fixed, halving r doubles ω², so ω grows by √2, not by 2.

It grows with R⁴, because I scales with R² and ω scales with R as well.
